overview: This is Congo-Brazzaville, the state west of the Congo River, distinct from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The map begins in 1945, while the territory was still under French rule. Independence came in 1960; modern Congolese history also includes painting, music, schools and changing urban life.

periods.title: From Middle Congo to independence
periods.summary: The French colonial territory became the independent Republic of the Congo on 15 August 1960.

periods.title: Independence and one-party government
periods.summary: Political upheaval followed independence; socialist one-party rule lasted from 1963 to 1991.

periods.title: A continuing republic
periods.summary: The 1991 National Conference introduced a multiparty transition. Later constitutional changes did not create a different people or erase the country’s institutions.

items.text: In 1958 the old framework of French Equatorial Africa was dismantled as its territories became republics. Congo’s full independence followed in August 1960. The map’s 1945 starting date therefore should not be read as an independence date.

The Congo-Océan railway linked inland Brazzaville with the Atlantic port of Pointe-Noire. Built under French colonial rule in the 1920s and completed in 1934, it crossed difficult terrain in the Mayombe region and became an important transport inheritance for the later state.

That railway carried an appalling human cost. The historical study describes coercive labour recruitment and more than 17,000 African deaths. A line on a transport map can conceal the lives and families whose labour made it possible.

Brazzaville’s Poto-Poto painting school began in 1951. Artists including Marcel Gotène helped make it an internationally recognized centre, where masters and younger painters worked within a continuing artistic community.

In March 2023 an exhibition brought together different generations of Poto-Poto-trained artists. The school had received UNESCO’s Picasso medal in 2002: its story continued well beyond the first famous painters.

Congolese rumba belongs to both Congo-Brazzaville and the neighbouring DRC. It accompanies celebrations and mourning, at home, in public and in religious settings. It is a shared musical culture crossing a state boundary.

Young rumba musicians can learn in neighbourhood clubs, training schools and community groups. Apprenticeship includes making instruments as well as playing them. Women helped shape important romantic and religious styles.

At Pointe-Noire’s École primaire 28 juin 1968, children once brought drinking water from home or bought it outside. UNICEF’s August 2022 account describes a new school water point. A tap can change an ordinary school day more than a grand monument.

The same school project involved a management committee with teachers, parents and community members. Children ran their own hygiene clubs, giving pupils responsibility for practical improvements around them.

At Brazzaville’s Bernadette Bayonne school, mothers Panive, Nadia and Berlude prepared meals for pupils in a 2021 canteen programme. The report says all 967 enrolled pupils could receive a daily meal; this is one documented school, not a nationwide count.

The canteen project also supplied handwashing equipment. Feeding children and providing a place to wash their hands were treated as parts of the same school environment, showing how education depends on everyday care as well as lessons.

A short written French sample is “Unité-Travail-Progrès”: “Unity, Work, Progress”, the motto in article 4 of the 2015 constitution. That article names French as official and Lingala and Kituba as national vehicular languages. The official document represents only one part of a multilingual country.

ending.text: The Republic of the Congo continues. Independence ended colonial government, while later political changes altered the state’s institutions. Its history has no final disappearance date.
